item: Federal estate tax basic exclusion amount — deaths in 2026
value: $15,000,000 per person
source_name: IRS — What's new: Estate and gift tax
quote: The Working Families Tax Cuts Bill (WFTC) was signed into law on July 4, 2025 as Public Law 119-21. WFTC amends § 2010(c)(3) by increasing the basic exclusion amount to $15,000,000 for calendar year 2026.
note: The IRS filing-threshold table on the Estate tax page shows the same figure for 2026.

item: Federal estate tax basic exclusion amount — deaths in 2027
value: $15,480,000 per person
source_name: IRS news release IR-2026-133 (Nov. 5, 2026)
quote: Estates of decedents who die during 2027 have a basic exclusion amount of $15,480,000, up from a total of $15,000,000 for estates of decedents who died in 2026.
note: Detail in Revenue Procedure 2026-35, section 3.44.

item: Form 706 filing threshold by year of death, 2011–2026 (shows how the exclusion has moved)
source_name: IRS — Estate tax
quote: A filing is required if the gross estate of the decedent, increased by the decedent’s adjusted taxable gifts and specific gift tax exemption, is valued at more than the filing threshold for the year of the decedent’s death, as shown in the table below. [...] 2017 $5,490,000; 2018 $11,180,000; [...] 2024 $13,610,000; 2025 $13,990,000; 2026 $15,000,000
note: Full table 2011–2026 is on the IRS page.

item: What counts toward the gross estate
value: Fair market value at date of death of cash, securities, real estate, insurance, trusts, annuities, business interests and other assets
source_name: IRS — Estate tax
quote: The fair market value of these items is used, not necessarily what you paid for them or what their values were when you acquired them. The total of all of these items is your "Gross Estate." The includible property may consist of cash and securities, real estate, insurance, trusts, annuities, business interests and other assets.
note: Both houses at market value (not assessed value) plus the cash count toward the threshold.

item: Portability — a surviving spouse can use the first spouse's unused exclusion
value: Election made on a timely filed Form 706 for the first spouse to die
source_name: IRS — Estate tax
quote: Beginning January 1, 2011, estates of decedents survived by a spouse may elect to pass any of the decedent's unused exemption to the surviving spouse. This election is made on a timely filed estate tax return for the decedent with a surviving spouse.
note: Only relevant if the current owners are a married couple; that is not stated in the brief.

item: Annual gift tax exclusion per recipient — 2026
source_name: IRS — Frequently asked questions on gift taxes
quote: The annual exclusion applies to gifts to each donee. In other words, if you give each of your children $19,000 in 2026, the annual exclusion applies to each gift. [table] 2026 | $19,000

item: Annual gift tax exclusion per recipient — 2027
source_name: IRS news release IR-2026-133 (Nov. 5, 2026)
quote: For calendar year 2027, the annual exclusion for gifts increases to $20,000, up from $19,000 for calendar year 2026.

item: Who pays gift tax
value: The donor (giver), not the recipient
source_name: IRS — Frequently asked questions on gift taxes
quote: The donor is generally responsible for paying the gift tax.

item: Basis of inherited property
value: Fair market value on the date of death (or alternate valuation date if elected on Form 706)
source_name: IRS FAQ — Gifts & inheritances
quote: The basis of property inherited from a decedent is generally one of the following: The fair market value (FMV) of the property on the date of the decedent's death (whether or not the executor of the estate files an estate tax return [...]). The FMV of the property on the alternate valuation date, but only if the executor of the estate files an estate tax return (Form 706) and elects to use the alternate valuation on that return.
note: This is the 'step-up in basis'.

item: Tax on selling inherited property
value: Only the amount above the date-of-death basis is taxable gain
source_name: IRS FAQ — Gifts & inheritances
quote: If you sell the property for more than your basis, you have a taxable gain.

item: Long-term capital gains rate structure
value: 0%, 15% or 20% depending on taxable income; up to 25% on unrecaptured section 1250 gain (prior depreciation on real property)
source_name: IRS Topic no. 409, Capital gains and losses
quote: Net capital gains are taxed at different rates depending on overall taxable income, although some or all net capital gain may be taxed at 0%. [...] However, a capital gains rate of 20% applies to the extent that your taxable income exceeds the thresholds set for the 15% capital gain rate. [...] The portion of any unrecaptured section 1250 gain from selling section 1250 real property is taxed at a maximum 25% rate.
note: The dollar thresholds printed on Topic 409 on the date checked are for tax year 2025; the 2027 thresholds are in row FED-CG-02.

item: Capital gains thresholds — tax year 2027
value: 0% up to $51,050 (single) / $102,100 (joint); 15% up to $563,200 (single) / $633,600 (joint); 20% above
source_name: IRS Revenue Procedure 2026-35, section 3.03
quote: For taxable years beginning in 2027, the maximum zero rate amounts and maximum 15 percent rate amounts under § 1(j)(5)(B), as adjusted for inflation, are as follows: Married Individuals Filing Joint Returns and Surviving Spouse $102,100 | $633,600; Married Individuals Filing Separate Returns $51,050 | $316,800; Heads of Households $68,350 | $598,400; All Other Individuals $51,050 | $563,200; Estates and Trusts $3,400 | $16,750

item: Losses on personal-use property
value: Not deductible
source_name: IRS Topic no. 409, Capital gains and losses
quote: Losses from the sale of personal-use property, such as your home or car, aren't tax deductible.

item: Ordinary income tax brackets — tax year 2027, married filing jointly
source_name: IRS Revenue Procedure 2026-35, section 3.01, Table 1
quote: Not over $25,600 | 10% of the taxable income; Over $25,600 but not over $104,050 | $2,560.00 plus 12% of the excess over $25,600; Over $104,050 but not over $218,250 | $11,974.00 plus 22% of the excess over $104,050; Over $218,250 but not over $416,650 | $37,098.00 plus 24% of the excess over $218,250; Over $416,650 but not over $529,100 | $84,714.00 plus 32% of the excess over $416,650; Over $529,100 but not over $793,650 | $120,698.00 plus 35% of the excess over $529,100; Over $793,650 | $213,290.50 plus 37% of the excess over $793,650

item: Ordinary income tax brackets — tax year 2027, single
source_name: IRS Revenue Procedure 2026-35, section 3.01, Table 3
quote: Not over $12,800 | 10% of the taxable income; Over $12,800 but not over $52,025 | $1,280.00 plus 12% of the excess over $12,800; Over $52,025 but not over $109,125 | $5,987.00 plus 22% of the excess over $52,025; Over $109,125 but not over $208,325 | $18,549.00 plus 24% of the excess over $109,125; Over $208,325 but not over $264,550 | $42,357.00 plus 32% of the excess over $208,325; Over $264,550 but not over $661,375 | $60,349.00 plus 35% of the excess over $264,550; Over $661,375 | $199,237.75 plus 37% of the excess over $661,375

item: Income tax brackets for trusts and estates — tax year 2027
source_name: IRS Revenue Procedure 2026-35, section 3.01, Table 5
quote: Not over $3,400 | 10% of the taxable income; Over $3,400 but not over $12,100 | $340 plus 24% of the excess over $3,400; Over $12,100 but not over $16,500 | $2,428 plus 35% of the excess over $12,100; Over $16,500 | $3,968 plus 37% of the excess over $16,500
note: Income kept inside a trust reaches the top rate very quickly; income distributed to the heir is taxed on the heir's return instead.

item: Home-sale exclusion (main home)
value: Up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 on a joint return)
source_name: IRS Topic no. 701, Sale of your home
quote: If you have a capital gain from the sale of your main home, you may qualify to exclude up to $250,000 of that gain from your income, or up to $500,000 of that gain if you file a joint return with your spouse.

item: Home-sale exclusion — ownership and use tests
value: Owned at least 2 years and lived in at least 2 years out of the 5 years before the sale
source_name: IRS Topic no. 701, Sale of your home
quote: If you or your spouse owned the home for at least 24 months (2 years) out of the last 5 years leading up to the date of the sale, you meet the ownership test. If you and your spouse used the home as a residence for at least 24 months (2 years) of the previous 5 years, you meet the use test.
note: Matters only for growth after the date of death, because the basis is reset at death.

item: Form 706 due date
value: 9 months after the date of death; automatic 6-month extension with Form 4768
source_name: IRS — Frequently asked questions on estate taxes
quote: The due date of the estate tax return is nine months after the decedent's date of death, however, the estate's representative may request an extension of time to file the return for up to six months. An automatic six month extension of time to file the return is available to all estates, including those filing solely to elect portability, by filing Form 4768 on or before the due date of the estate tax return.

item: When Form 706 must be filed
value: Gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts above the year's threshold, or whenever portability is elected
source_name: IRS — Frequently asked questions on estate taxes
quote: An estate tax return (Form 706) must be filed if the gross estate of the decedent (who is a U.S. citizen or resident), increased by the decedent’s adjusted taxable gifts and specific gift tax exemption, is valued at more than the filing threshold for the year of the decedent’s death [...] An estate tax return also must be filed if the estate elects to transfer any deceased spousal unused exclusion (DSUE) amount to a surviving spouse, regardless of the size of the gross estate or amount of adjusted taxable gifts.

item: Late portability election (estate below the filing threshold)
value: Simplified method: complete Form 706 filed on or before the fifth anniversary of the death
source_name: IRS — Frequently asked questions on estate taxes
quote: The simplified method under the revenue procedure to obtain an extension of time to make the portability election requires the filing of a complete and properly prepared estate tax return on or before the fifth annual anniversary of the decedent’s date of death and requires a notation on the estate tax return that the return is “FILED PURSUANT TO REV. PROC. 2022-32 TO ELECT PORTABILITY UNDER § 2010(c)(5)(A).”

item: Net investment income tax (NIIT)
value: 3.8% on the lesser of net investment income or MAGI above $200,000 (single / head of household) or $250,000 (joint)
source_name: IRS Topic no. 559, Net investment income tax
quote: In the case of an individual, the NIIT is 3.8 percent on the lesser of: the net investment income, or the excess of modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) over the following threshold amounts: $250,000 for married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse; $125,000 for married filing separately; $200,000 for single or head of household
note: These thresholds are not indexed for inflation in the IRS text.

item: What NIIT covers
value: Interest, dividends, rents and net gains from selling stocks, bonds, funds and real estate
source_name: IRS Topic no. 559, Net investment income tax
quote: In general, net investment income for purpose of this tax, includes, but isn't limited to: interest, dividends, certain annuities, royalties, and rents (unless derived in a trade or business in which the NIIT doesn't apply), [...] net gains from the disposition of property such as stocks, bonds, mutual funds, and real estate (to the extent taken into account in computing taxable income), other than property held in a trade or business to which NIIT doesn't apply

item: Rental income is taxable; expenses are deductible
value: Report on Schedule E; depreciation, repairs and operating expenses are deductible
source_name: IRS Topic no. 414, Rental income and expenses
quote: Cash or the fair market value of property or services you receive for the use of real estate or personal property is taxable to you as rental income. In general, you can deduct expenses of renting property from your rental income. [...] You can generally use Schedule E (Form 1040), Supplemental Income and Loss to report income and expenses related to real estate rentals.

item: Qualified business income deduction for rentals
value: Possible additional deduction of 20% of qualified business income if the safe-harbor requirements are met
source_name: IRS Topic no. 414, Rental income and expenses
quote: In addition to your qualified rental expenses, you may be eligible to deduct an additional 20% of your qualified business income (QBI) if you meet all of the safe harbor requirements; refer to Revenue Procedure 2019-38
note: Not modelled in the projections (eligibility depends on hours of rental services).

item: Rental profit can also be subject to NIIT
value: Yes
source_name: IRS Topic no. 414, Rental income and expenses
quote: If you have a rental profit, you may be subject to the net investment income tax (NIIT).

item: Federal estate tax rate on the amount above the exclusion
value: 40% (top bracket of the statutory schedule, reached at $1,000,000 of taxable amount; the exclusion works as a credit that covers the lower brackets)
source_name: 26 U.S.C. § 2001(c) (U.S. Code, 2024 edition, U.S. Government Publishing Office)
quote: Over $1,000,000 | $345,800, plus 40 percent of the excess of such amount over $1,000,000.
note: The same 40% line appears in Table A of the IRS Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. July 2026).

item: Statute: basis of property acquired from a decedent
value: Fair market value at the date of death
source_name: 26 U.S.C. § 1014(a) (U.S. Code, 2024 edition, U.S. Government Publishing Office)
quote: the basis of property in the hands of a person acquiring the property from a decedent or to whom the property passed from a decedent shall, if not sold, exchanged, or otherwise disposed of before the decedent's death by such person, be— (1) the fair market value of the property at the date of the decedent's death

item: Property in a revocable (living) trust qualifies for the date-of-death basis
value: Yes — listed in § 1014(b)(2)
source_name: 26 U.S.C. § 1014(b)(2) (U.S. Code, 2024 edition, U.S. Government Publishing Office)
quote: (2) Property transferred by the decedent during his lifetime in trust to pay the income for life to or on the order or direction of the decedent, with the right reserved to the decedent at all times before his death to revoke the trust;
note: The brief says 'by trust' but not which kind; see the flag on trust type.

item: Property in an irrevocable trust that is NOT included in the owner's gross estate
value: No basis reset at death — the old basis carries over
source_name: IRS Revenue Ruling 2023-2
quote: If A funds T with Asset in a transaction that is a completed gift for gift tax purposes, the basis of Asset is not adjusted to its fair market value on the date of A’s death under § 1014 because Asset was not acquired or passed from a decedent as defined in § 1014(b). Accordingly, under this revenue ruling’s facts, the basis of Asset immediately after A’s death is the same as the basis of Asset immediately prior to A’s death.
note: This is why the type of trust is the first thing to confirm.

item: Community property: surviving spouse's half also gets the date-of-death basis
value: Yes, if at least half of the community interest was included in the decedent's gross estate
source_name: 26 U.S.C. § 1014(b)(6) (U.S. Code, 2024 edition, U.S. Government Publishing Office)
quote: (6) In the case of decedents dying after December 31, 1947, property which represents the surviving spouse's one-half share of community property held by the decedent and the surviving spouse under the community property laws of any State, or possession of the United States or any foreign country, if at least one-half of the whole of the community interest in such property was includible in determining the value of the decedent's gross estate
note: Only relevant if the current owners are spouses holding community property; not stated in the brief.

item: If an estate tax return is filed, the heir's basis cannot exceed the estate-tax value
value: Basis must be consistent with the value finally determined for estate tax
source_name: 26 U.S.C. § 1014(f) (U.S. Code, 2024 edition, U.S. Government Publishing Office)
quote: The basis of any property to which subsection (a) applies shall not exceed— (A) in the case of property the final value of which has been determined for purposes of the tax imposed by chapter 11 on the estate of such decedent, such value

item: Prop 19 parent-to-child exclusion — which property qualifies
value: Only a family home that is the principal residence of the parent AND becomes the principal residence of the child (or a family farm)
source_name: California State Board of Equalization — Proposition 19 (comparison chart)
quote: Principal Residence | [Proposition 19 (Current Law)] Principal residence of transferor and transferee; Value limit of current taxable value plus $1,000,000 (as biennially adjusted); Family homes and farms. Other Real Property | Eliminates exclusion for other real property other than the principal residence
note: Effective for transfers on or after February 16, 2021.

item: Prop 19 — a rental home passed from parent to child
value: Does not qualify; it is reassessed
source_name: California State Board of Equalization — Proposition 19, Parent-Child FAQ 4
quote: No, Proposition 19 limits the parent-child transfer exclusion to a transfer of (1) a family home that is the principal residence of the transferor and becomes the principal residence of the transferee, or (2) a family farm. Thus, the transfer of a rental home between parents and children would not qualify for the exclusion.

item: Prop 19 — value limit when the home is worth more than the cap
value: Excluded amount = factored base year value + the '$1 million amount'; market value above that is added to the factored base year value
source_name: California State Board of Equalization — Proposition 19, Parent-Child FAQ 6
quote: The value limit under Proposition 19 is the sum of the factored base year value plus $1 million. If the market value exceeds this limit, the amount exceeding the value limit will be added to the factored base year value. [...] For example, a family home has a factored base year value (FBYV) of $300,000 and a fair market value of $1,500,000. The excluded amount under Proposition 19 is $1,300,000 ($300,000 + $1,000,000 = $1,300,000). The difference of $200,000 ($1,500,000 - $1,300,000 = $200,000) is added to the property's FBYV. Thus, the adjusted base year value is $500,000
note: Arithmetically the new taxable value equals market value minus the '$1 million amount' whenever market value is above the cap.

item: Prop 19 — current '$1 million amount'
value: $1,044,586 for transfers from February 16, 2025 through February 15, 2027
source_name: State Board of Equalization, Letter To Assessors No. 2025/009 (March 7, 2025)
quote: Accordingly, the $1 million amount is adjusted to $1,044,586. Consequently, for transfers that occur February 16, 2025 through February 15, 2027, the value cap will be the sum of the property's factored base year value plus $1,044,586.

item: Prop 19 — how the '$1 million amount' is indexed
value: Every other February 16, by the percentage change in the FHFA House Price Index for California for the prior calendar year (one year's change every two years)
source_name: State Board of Equalization, Letter To Assessors No. 2025/009 (quoting Cal. Const. art. XIII A, § 2.1(c)(4))
quote: Beginning on February 16, 2023, and every other February 16 thereafter, the State Board of Equalization shall adjust the one million dollar ($1,000,000) amount described in paragraph (1) for inflation to reflect the percentage change in the House Price Index for California for the prior calendar year, as determined by the Federal Housing Finance Agency. [...] The next adjustment of the $1 million amount will occur in February 2027.
note: 2023 adjustment +2.26%, 2025 adjustment +2.15% (FHFA change for 2024). Because only one year's change is applied every second year, the amount rises more slowly than house prices.

item: Prop 19 — deadline to move in
value: The home must become the child's principal residence within one year after the transfer; no exceptions
source_name: State Board of Equalization, Letter To Assessors No. 2026/026 (August 3, 2026), Question 7
quote: Yes, the transfer is required to be of a principal residence of the transferor that qualifies as the principal residence of the transferee within one year after the transfer under section 63.2(a)(1)(A). There are no exceptions to this rule.

item: Prop 19 — claim forms and deadlines
value: Homeowners' exemption claim (BOE-266) within 1 year of the death; exclusion claim (BOE-19-P) within 3 years or before any transfer to a third party, whichever is earlier
source_name: State Board of Equalization, Letter To Assessors No. 2026/026 (August 3, 2026), Filing Requirements
quote: First, the transferee must file for the Homeowners' or Disabled Veterans' Exemption within one year of the date of purchase or transfer to be considered timely. The transferee must also file for the appropriate intergenerational transfer exclusion within three years of the date of purchase or transfer, or before a transfer to a third party, whichever is earlier.
note: Form names from the BOE Proposition 19 filing checklist: BOE-266 Claim for Homeowners' Property Tax Exemption; BOE-19-P Claim for Reassessment Exclusion for Transfer Between Parent and Child Occurring on or After February 16, 2021. Both are filed with the county assessor.

item: Prop 19 — if the heir later moves out
value: Exclusion is removed; taxable value becomes the market value on the date of inheritance, adjusted for the annual inflation factor
source_name: California State Board of Equalization — Proposition 19, Parent-Child FAQ 3
quote: At least one eligible transferee must continually live in the property as their family home for the property to maintain the exclusion. Thus, once the property is no longer your principal residence, it will receive a new taxable value as of the lien date following the date you no longer occupy the property as your principal residence. The new taxable value will be the fair market value of the home on the date you inherited it, adjusted each year after for the inflation factor, and enrolled as of the lien date following the date you moved out.

item: Prop 19 — property held in a trust
value: The change in ownership date is the date of death (when the revocable trust becomes irrevocable)
source_name: California State Board of Equalization — Proposition 19, Parent-Child FAQ 9
quote: For properties held in trusts, Revenue and Taxation Code section 61(h) provides that a change in ownership occurs when any interests in real property vest in persons other than the trustor or the trustor's spouse or registered domestic partner when a revocable trust becomes irrevocable [...] This typically occurs upon the death of the trustor. Thus, the date of death is considered to be the date of change in ownership.
note: All one-year and three-year clocks start on the date of death, not on the date the deed is recorded.

item: Prop 19 — parent in a hospital or care facility before death
value: Home is still treated as the parent's principal residence if the parent would live there, intends to return, and it is not rented to anyone other than an immediate family member
source_name: State Board of Equalization, Letter To Assessors No. 2026/026 (August 3, 2026), Question 11
quote: If a person receiving the exemption is not occupying the dwelling because they are confined to a hospital or other care facility, the person is deemed to occupy that dwelling as their principal place of residence, provided all the following are met: The person would occupy the dwelling if they were not confined to the hospital or other care facility. The person intends to return to the dwelling when possible to do so. The dwelling is not rented or leased to anyone other than an immediate family member.
note: Renting Property A to a non-family tenant before the inheritance would put the exclusion at risk.

item: Prop 19 — one child, two homes
value: Only one home can be the child's principal residence, so only one can receive the exclusion
source_name: State Board of Equalization, Letter To Assessors No. 2026/026 (August 3, 2026), Question 2
quote: If, however, the parent transferred both principal residences to the same child, and that child retained both residences, only one can qualify as the child's principal residence and thus qualify for the intergenerational transfer exclusion.
note: The heir cannot keep a primary residence in Property B and also claim the exclusion on Property A.

item: Prop 19 — multi-unit building
value: Only the unit the parent lived in (and the child then lives in) can qualify; the other units are reassessed to market value
source_name: State Board of Equalization, Letter To Assessors No. 2026/026 (August 3, 2026), Questions 5 and 15
quote: No, only the unit occupied as the principal residence qualifies as the principal residence of the transferor. The remainder of the apartment complex would be ineligible for the intergenerational transfer exclusion and would be reassessed at its full cash value as of the date of transfer. [...] For intergenerational transfer exclusions under Proposition 19, each unit of a multi-unit or multi-family property is considered a separate principal residence. Each unit must individually qualify for the intergenerational exclusion.
note: Applies to Property B only if Property B is also still owned by the current owner and passes by inheritance; the brief does not say who owns Property B today.

item: Prop 19 — claim filed late
value: Relief only from the lien date of the year the claim is filed (no refund for earlier years)
source_name: State Board of Equalization, Letter To Assessors No. 2026/026 (August 3, 2026), Filing Requirements
quote: If all deadlines have expired and the transferee still owns the property, the transferee may file a claim and receive prospective relief only. Prospective relief applies to the lien date of the assessment year in which the claim is filed.

item: Prop 19 — bills to restore the old parent-child exclusion listed by the BOE
value: Assembly Constitutional Amendment 9 (2021-22) and Senate Constitutional Amendment 4 (2023-24) are listed; neither changed the law
source_name: California State Board of Equalization — Proposition 19 (Legislation tab)
quote: Senate Constitutional Amendment 4 | Property Taxation: Principal Residence and Family Home Transfers | Seyarto [...] Assembly Constitutional Amendment 9 | Transfers of Principal Residences | Kiley
note: The BOE page lists them under past sessions; Proposition 19 remains 'Current Law' on the same page.

item: Prop 13 — annual increase in assessed (base year) value
value: Inflation factor from the California CPI, capped at 2% a year
source_name: State Board of Equalization, Letter To Assessors No. 2026/002 (January 13, 2026)
quote: Revenue and Taxation Code section 51 provides that base year values determined under section 110.1 shall be compounded annually by an inflation factor, not to exceed 2 percent.

item: Prop 13 — inflation factor for the 2026 roll (fiscal year 2026-27)
value: 1.02 (California CPI rose 3.307%, capped at 2%)
source_name: State Board of Equalization, Letter To Assessors No. 2026/002 (January 13, 2026)
quote: Information from the DIR shows that the CCPI increased from 343.108 in August 2024 to 354.456 in August 2025. Rounded to the nearest one-thousandth of 1 percent, this is an increase of 3.307 percent. Accordingly, please prepare your 2026 assessment roll using an inflation factor of 1.02.
note: The factor for the 2027 roll had not been published by the BOE on the date checked.

item: Prop 13 — history of the inflation factor, 1976-77 to 2026-27
source_name: State Board of Equalization, Letter To Assessors No. 2026/002 (January 13, 2026), enclosure
note: Full table stored in integration/ledger/prop13_factors.json. The yearly percentage changes in the owner-supplied assessment histories (2%, 1.5%, 1%, 0.5%) line up with these official factors for every year supplied.

item: Reassessment when ownership changes
value: Reassessed to current fair market value as of the date ownership changed; inheritance counts as a transfer
source_name: State Board of Equalization — Change in Ownership, Frequently Asked Questions
quote: A transfer can be a sale or purchase, but it also can be a gift or inheritance. [...] Once the county assessor has determined that a change in ownership has occurred, Proposition 13 requires the county assessor to reassess the property to its current fair market value as of the date ownership changed.

item: Deadline to report a change in ownership caused by a death (no probate)
value: Within 150 days of the date of death
source_name: State Board of Equalization — Change in Ownership, Frequently Asked Questions
quote: If the change in ownership was the result of a death and there is no probate: Within 150 days of the date of death
note: Revenue and Taxation Code section 480.

item: Penalty for not filing a Change in Ownership Statement after the assessor asks for it
value: $100 or 10% of the taxes on the new base year value, whichever is greater; capped at $5,000 if the property is eligible for the homeowners' exemption, $20,000 if not
source_name: State Board of Equalization — Change in Ownership, Frequently Asked Questions
quote: The penalty for failure to file a Change in Ownership Statement upon a written request by the Assessor is $100 or 10 percent of the taxes applicable to the new base year value reflecting the change in ownership of the real property, manufactured home, or floating home, whichever is greater, but such penalty may not exceed $5,000 if the property is eligible for the homeowners' exemption or $20,000 if the property is not eligible for the homeowners' exemption, unless the failure to file was willful.

item: Unreported change in ownership — how far back the assessor can bill
value: Up to eight prior assessment rolls
source_name: State Board of Equalization — Change in Ownership, Frequently Asked Questions
quote: the county assessor must retroactively assess as many as eight prior assessment rolls if the escape assessment was the result of the failure to file a required Change in Ownership Statement.

item: Homeowners' exemption
value: $7,000 reduction in taxable value for an owner-occupied principal residence (one-time filing, form BOE-266)
source_name: State Board of Equalization — Homeowners' Exemption
quote: The California Constitution provides a $7,000 reduction in the taxable value for a qualifying owner-occupied home. The home must have been the principal place of residence of the owner on the lien date, January 1st.
note: Worth roughly $70–$80 a year at a rate a little above 1%.
